questions.question: What is the main benefit of externalized configuration?
options: The same jar can run with different settings in different environments
The app no longer needs Java to run
Settings are stored inside the compiled classes
questions.explanation: Settings live outside the code, so one build can be configured differently for laptop, test and production.

questions.question: Which of these sources has the HIGHEST priority in Spring Boot?
options: A config/application.properties file next to the jar
A command line argument such as --server.port=9000
questions.explanation: Command line arguments sit near the top of the priority list, above environment variables and all files.

questions.question: The jar has cinema.ticket-price=200. It is started with CINEMA_TICKET_PRICE=250 and the argument --cinema.ticket-price=300. Which price does the app use?
questions.explanation: The command line argument beats the environment variable, which in turn beats the file in the jar.

questions.question: Which environment variable overrides the key clinic.max-tokens?
questions.explanation: Spring Boot maps upper case names with underscores, so CLINIC_MAX_TOKENS matches clinic.max-tokens.

questions.question: A developer edits application.properties on the server, but the running app still shows the old value. What is the most likely reason?
options: The file is packed inside the jar, so the copy on disk is not read
Properties files are ignored in production
The value must be written in upper case
Spring Boot only reads YAML files on servers
questions.explanation: The file inside the jar is sealed, and settings are read at startup. Use a config folder beside the jar and restart.
